summary.text: Take the composite number \(n=23492890653051=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341\), whose factors are prime.  Multiplicativity of the gcd-sum and the prime formula \(\sum_{k=1}^{p}\gcd(k,p)=2p-1\) give \(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(k,n)=610815156979325\), so adding 1 yields \(610815156979326=26n\); hence the denominator gcd is \(n\) and the resulting quotient is \(1\), despite \(n\) being composite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
G(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(k,n),
\qquad
a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,1+G(n))}.
\]
We will exhibit a composite integer \(n>1\) for which \(a(n)=1\).

The counterexample is
\[
n=23492890653051
  =3\cdot 37\cdot 43\cdot 42307\cdot 116341.
\]
We first establish the formula that will allow us to evaluate its gcd-sum.

For every positive integer \(n\), group the integers \(k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) according to the value \(d=\gcd(k,n)\). Such a value \(d\) must divide \(n\). If \(d\mid n\), then \(\gcd(k,n)=d\) precisely when \(k=dj\), where
\[
1\leq j\leq n/d
\quad\text{and}\quad
\gcd(j,n/d)=1.
\]
There are \(\varphi(n/d)\) such integers \(j\), with the usual convention \(\varphi(1)=1\). Every member of this class contributes \(d\) to the sum. Consequently,
\[
G(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\,\varphi(n/d). \tag{1}
\]

The right-hand side is multiplicative. Indeed, if \(m\) and \(n\) are coprime, every divisor of \(mn\) has a unique form \(d_1d_2\), with \(d_1\mid m\) and \(d_2\mid n\). Moreover, \(m/d_1\) and \(n/d_2\) are coprime, so the multiplicativity of Euler's totient gives
\[
\varphi\!\left(\frac{mn}{d_1d_2}\right)
 =\varphi(m/d_1)\varphi(n/d_2).
\]
Substitution in (1) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(mn)
 &=\sum_{d_1\mid m}\sum_{d_2\mid n}
 d_1d_2\,\varphi(m/d_1)\varphi(n/d_2)\\
 &=\left(\sum_{d_1\mid m}d_1\varphi(m/d_1)\right)
   \left(\sum_{d_2\mid n}d_2\varphi(n/d_2)\right)\\
 &=G(m)G(n).
\end{aligned} \tag{2}
\]
For a prime \(p\), the only divisors in (1) are \(1\) and \(p\). Therefore
\[
G(p)=\varphi(p)+p\varphi(1)=(p-1)+p=2p-1. \tag{3}
\]

For completeness, we verify that all five displayed factors of the proposed counterexample are prime. The primality of \(3\), \(37\), and \(43\) follows immediately by trial division: a composite number has a prime divisor no greater than its square root; neither \(37\) nor \(43\) is divisible by any of \(2,3,5\), and both have square root less than \(7\).

We use the following standard form of Pocklington's criterion for the two larger factors. Suppose \(N>1\), and a completely factored integer \(F\) divides \(N-1\), with \(F>\sqrt N\). If, for every prime \(q\mid F\), there is an integer \(b\) such that
\[
b^{N-1}\equiv1\pmod N
\quad\text{and}\quad
\gcd\bigl(b^{(N-1)/q}-1,N\bigr)=1,
\]
then \(N\) is prime. To see why, let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(N\). The first congruence says that the order of \(b\) modulo \(r\) divides \(N-1\), while the gcd condition says that it does not divide \((N-1)/q\). Taking account of every prime power in \(F\), this forces \(F\) to divide the order, and hence to divide \(r-1\). Thus every prime divisor \(r\) of \(N\) is greater than \(F>\sqrt N\). A composite \(N\) would have a prime divisor at most \(\sqrt N\), a contradiction.

For \(N=42307\), we have the complete factorization
\[
N-1=42306=2\cdot3\cdot11\cdot641.
\]
The number \(641\) is prime: \(\sqrt{641}<26\), and division by the primes \(2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23\) gives respective remainders
\[
1,2,1,4,3,4,12,14,20,
\]
all nonzero. Thus all prime factors occurring in this factorization of \(N-1\) are known. Take \(b=3\). Modular exponentiation gives
\[
3^{42306}\equiv1\pmod{42307},
\]
and the residues required for the distinct prime divisors of \(N-1\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&(N-1)/q&3^{(N-1)/q}\pmod N\\ \hline
2&21153&42306\\
3&14102&36715\\
11&3846&17937\\
641&66&10961
\end{array}
\]
These modular calculations can be checked directly by repeated squaring. For transparency, the successive residues \(3^{2^i}\pmod{42307}\), for \(i=0,1,\ldots,15\), are
\[
3,9,81,6561,20502,11959,20021,23923,
23140,22208,22565,14480,39215,41389,38891,34631.
\]
Multiplying those entries selected by the binary expansion of each exponent gives the residues in the table.

The required gcds are all \(1\). Explicit Bézout identities, which also check that assertion without any hidden divisibility assumption, are
\[
\begin{aligned}
21153(42306-1)-21152(42307)&=1,\\
-12239(36715-1)+10621(42307)&=1,\\
6088(17937-1)-2581(42307)&=1,\\
-6651(10961-1)+1723(42307)&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(F=N-1>\sqrt N\), Pocklington's criterion proves that \(42307\) is prime.

For \(N=116341\), similarly,
\[
N-1=116340=2^2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot277.
\]
The number \(277\) is prime because \(\sqrt{277}<17\), and its remainders upon division by \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) are respectively
\[
1,1,2,4,2,4,
\]
so it has no prime divisor at most its square root. Take \(b=14\). Modular exponentiation gives
\[
14^{116340}\equiv1\pmod{116341},
\]
and
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&(N-1)/q&14^{(N-1)/q}\pmod N\\ \hline
2&58170&116340\\
3&38780&50801\\
5&23268&81650\\
7&16620&10889\\
277&420&35125
\end{array}
\]
Again, these are ordinary repeated-squaring calculations. The successive residues \(14^{2^i}\pmod{116341}\), for \(i=0,1,\ldots,16\), are
\[
14,196,38416,3471,64718,27183,33798,68866,1432,
72827,18421,82885,103516,90792,78391,17261,109161.
\]
They give the displayed values by multiplying according to the binary expansions of the exponents.

The gcd conditions follow from the Bézout identities
\[
\begin{aligned}
58170(116340-1)-58169(116341)&=1,\\
21846(50801-1)-9539(116341)&=1,\\
-15490(81650-1)+10871(116341)&=1,\\
-9200(10889-1)+861(116341)&=1,\\
-9026(35125-1)+2725(116341)&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus Pocklington's criterion proves that \(116341\) is prime.

The five factors \(3,37,43,42307,116341\) are distinct primes, hence pairwise coprime. Their product can be checked in stages:
\[
3\cdot37=111,
\quad111\cdot43=4773,
\quad4773\cdot42307=201931311,
\]
followed by
\[
201931311\cdot116341=23492890653051=n.
\]
We may therefore apply multiplicativity (2), followed by (3), to obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(n)
&=(2\cdot3-1)(2\cdot37-1)(2\cdot43-1)
  (2\cdot42307-1)(2\cdot116341-1)\\
&=5\cdot73\cdot85\cdot84613\cdot232681.
\end{aligned}
\]
The arithmetic product is
\[
5\cdot73=365,
\qquad365\cdot85=31025,
\]
\[
31025\cdot84613=2625118325,
\]
and finally
\[
2625118325\cdot232681=610815156979325.
\]
Thus
\[
G(n)=610815156979325.
\]
Adding one gives
\[
1+G(n)=610815156979326.
\]
But direct multiplication shows
\[
26n=26\cdot23492890653051=610815156979326.
\]
Therefore \(1+G(n)=26n\), and since \(n>0\),
\[
\gcd(n,1+G(n))=\gcd(n,26n)=n.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,1+G(n))}=\frac{n}{n}=1.
\]

On the other hand, \(n\neq1\), and \(n\) is not prime: explicitly,
\[
n=3\cdot7830963551017,
\]
where both factors are greater than \(1\). We have therefore found a positive composite integer \(n>1\) for which \(a(n)=1\). Hence the assertion that \(a(n)=1\) holds if and only if \(n=1\) or \(n\) is prime is false.
